what_changed.headline: PCE inflation rose to 3.6% in September, and Q3 economic growth came in at a strong 3.4% annual pace.
items: PCE prices (the Fed's official target) increased from +3.4% to +3.6% in the year to September.
Core PCE (without food and energy) edged up from +3.0% to +3.1% in the year to September.

Real consumer spending flattened to +0.0% in September, while real after-tax income dipped −0.3%.

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 3.75% to 4.00%. The Fed just held in October, but more rises remain likely later this year.
verdict.confidence_note: “Medium” means the Fed just held at the October meeting, but strong inflation and two dissenting votes keep the door open for December.
verdict.short_version: The Fed held its rate steady in October by a 10-2 vote. With inflation still above target, markets are now looking toward December to see if the Fed will raise rates again.
verdict.card_why: The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4.00% in October, but two officials wanted a rise and inflation remains elevated.

why_steps.title: The Fed has two jobs, and one main tool
why_steps.html: By law, the Fed tries to do two things at the same time: keep prices steady and keep jobs plentiful. For prices, its target is that things should cost about 2% more each year, which is slow enough that people barely notice. Its main tool is its interest rate, the cost of borrowing money. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas: loans get cheaper, spending picks up, and companies hire more. Holding means keeping your foot where it is.

why_steps.title: Right now, prices are the bigger problem
why_steps.html: Prices are rising about 3.6% a year, measured by the Fed's preferred price gauge, called PCE (the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index from the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost $100 a year ago now costs about $103.60. The goal would be about $102. The main cause is energy. Conflict in the Middle East pushed up oil prices this year, with WTI crude reaching $103.37 a barrel in late October. Regular gasoline averaged $4.269 a gallon in late October, compared with roughly $3.12 a year earlier. Energy matters for everything, because trucks carry food to shops, factories run machines, and airlines burn fuel, so higher energy costs slowly spread into the price of almost everything. Fed officials point out that prices have now been above the 2% goal for more than five years, and they worry people will start to expect high inflation as normal.

why_steps.title: The Fed held in October, but dissenters wanted a rise
why_steps.html: On October 28, the Fed voted 10–2 to hold its rate steady at 3.75%–4.00%. Two officials—Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack—voted against the hold, preferring to raise the rate by 0.25 percentage points right away. In its official statement, the Fed noted that economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, domestic spending is resilient, and inflation remains elevated. There is only one meeting left this year: December 8–9.

why_steps.title: Reasons the Fed chose to wait in October
why_steps.html:
• Hiring has slowed sharply. Only 29,000 jobs were added in September, and July was revised to a loss of 10,000 jobs. When hiring is weak, pressing the brake again right away raises the risk of layoffs.
  • The market already pressed the brake for them. The interest rate on 10-year U.S. government bonds rose to 4.98% in late October. Mortgages and many business loans follow that rate. So borrowing has already become more expensive, which cools the economy without the Fed doing anything.
  • Senior officials hinted there is no rush. Governor Christopher Waller said rate rises do not need to come at consecutive meetings. Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said reaching a decision may take more time.
  • The brake takes time to work. A rate change takes many months to fully affect the economy. The Fed only raised in September and wanted to see the effect first.

why_steps.title: Why a December rise remains very possible
why_steps.html:
• Inflation is too high and not improving. The official statement noted that inflation remains elevated and the Fed will deliver price stability.
  • Two officials dissented. Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voted to raise rates in October, showing real appetite inside the Fed to keep tightening.
  • The economy is strong enough to handle it. Q3 real GDP growth came in at 3.4% at an annual pace. A strong economy can absorb a higher rate.
  • The Fed has made a public promise. Its statements emphasize that the Committee will deliver price stability. Acting in December can make that promise more believable if inflation does not cool.

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Two officials dissented to raise in October
right: “No rush” hints from Waller and Jefferson

why_steps.html: Both sides are strong. What tipped the scale toward Hold in October was that the Fed wanted time to assess its September move and watch incoming data. But with two dissenters and high inflation, December remains wide open.

why_steps.title: The one thing to watch: upcoming growth and price reports
why_steps.html: The Bureau of Labor Statistics and the Commerce Department publish major economic reports right after the October meeting, including Q3 GDP growth and September PCE prices on October 29. These reports will not change the October decision, but they will heavily shape whether the Fed decides to raise rates at the December meeting.

timeline.title: The Fed cut its rate three times
timeline.what: The Fed lowered its rate by 0.25 points in September, October and December 2025, taking it from 4.25%–4.50% down to 3.50%–3.75%.
timeline.why: Hiring had slowed, and the Fed worried that people could start losing jobs. Inflation looked like it was slowly coming under control, so the Fed felt safe pressing the gas a little.
timeline.people: Borrowing got a bit cheaper (for example on credit cards and car loans), and interest earned on savings accounts dipped.
timeline.because: the Fed decided to pause and watch. Rate cuts take months to work, so it wanted to see their effect before doing more.

timeline.title: A pause: the rate stayed at 3.50%–3.75%
timeline.what: The Fed held its rate. Its statement described inflation as somewhat elevated and said job gains had remained low. Two voters wanted another cut.
timeline.why: The Fed was balancing two worries: jobs were soft, but prices were still a little too high. Holding was the middle path.
timeline.people: Not much change. Loan and savings rates stayed about the same. At this point, most debate was about when to cut again, not about raising.
timeline.because: the Fed was sitting still when a new problem arrived: trouble in the Middle East started pushing up energy prices.

timeline.title: An energy shock: prices start climbing again
timeline.what: The Fed held in March and April. In April it said inflation was elevated in part reflecting the recent increase in global energy prices. Three voters objected to the statement still hinting at future cuts.
timeline.why: When oil gets expensive, it does not just raise gasoline prices. It raises the cost of shipping, farming, flying and making things, so prices across the economy creep up.
timeline.people: Filling the car and heating the home got noticeably more expensive. Families with lower incomes and people in rural areas, who drive more, felt it most.
timeline.because: the mood inside the Fed shifted. Instead of asking when do we cut?, officials began asking should we stop talking about cuts at all?

timeline.title: A new leader at the Fed
timeline.what: Kevin Warsh became Chair of the Fed. The previous Chair, Jerome Powell, stayed on the Board as a Governor.
timeline.people: Nothing changed immediately, but markets paid close attention to how the new leadership would respond to rising prices.
timeline.because: the next meetings were led by a new Chair, facing the same energy-driven price problem.

timeline.title: Still holding, but pressure to raise grows
timeline.what: In June all 12 voters agreed to hold, and the statement added a firm line: The Committee will deliver price stability. In July the Fed held again, but this time three voters wanted to raise the rate.
timeline.why: Prices kept running hot. The hint about future cuts was gone, replaced by a promise to bring prices down. Some officials felt that words were not enough and action was needed.
timeline.people: The chance of cheaper loans soon faded. Savers kept earning similar rates. Bond markets started to expect rate rises.
timeline.because: everyone watched the August data closely to see whether prices would calm down on their own. They did not.

timeline.title: Prices hot, spending strong, jobs okay
timeline.what: Consumer prices (CPI) were up 3.7% from a year earlier, with energy alone up 20.4%. The Fed's preferred gauge (PCE) was also up 3.4%, and 3.0% without food and energy. Shop sales jumped 0.8% in September. The economy grew at a 2.2% yearly pace in spring.
timeline.people: Paychecks were rising about 3% a year, roughly the same as prices, so many families felt they were running just to stand still.
timeline.because: the Fed concluded that waiting was no longer enough.

timeline.title: The Fed raised its rate to 3.75%–4.00%
timeline.what: The first rise in this cycle, by 0.25 points. All 12 voters agreed. The Fed said this will support a timelier return to 2% inflation.
timeline.people: Rates on credit cards and many variable loans went up a little. Savings accounts and short-term deposits started paying slightly more.
timeline.because: investors expected more rises to come, so longer-term borrowing costs in the market rose too.

timeline.title: Market interest rates jumped
timeline.what: The interest rate on 10-year U.S. government bonds rose to 4.98%. The 2-year rate stood at 4.61%.
timeline.why: When investors expect the Fed to keep rates high and prices to stay high, they demand more interest to lend money for years at a time.
timeline.people: Mortgage rates and many business loan rates follow the 10-year rate, so buying a house or expanding a business got more expensive within weeks.
timeline.because: the economy started to feel tighter even without another Fed move. Some officials began saying they could take their time.

timeline.title: A weak jobs report for September
timeline.what: Only 29,000 jobs were added. Unemployment ticked up from 4.1% to 4.2%. But weekly claims for unemployment benefits stayed very low (194,000).
timeline.people: If you have a job, it is fairly safe. If you are looking for one, it has become harder to find.
timeline.because: the case for raising rates again right away became weaker, because pressing the brake too hard on a slowing job market is risky.

timeline.title: The Fed held its rate at 3.75%–4.00%
timeline.what: The Fed maintained the target range at 3.75%–4.00% by a 10–2 vote. Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissented, preferring a 0.25 point rise.
timeline.why: The Fed balanced elevated inflation against recent weak hiring and higher market bond yields, choosing to pause while keeping future rises on the table.
timeline.people: Loan and savings rates remained steady for the moment, while markets turned their attention to December.
timeline.because: our reading is that the Fed will likely hold or consider further hikes in December as incoming data clarifies inflation trends.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 3.75%–4.00%
choices.meaning: the Fed keeps its foot where it is on the brake, choosing to assess incoming economic reports before making its next move.
for: Weak hiring. September added only 29,000 jobs. The Fed does not want to cause layoffs by braking too hard, too fast.
The market did some of the work. Higher bond rates already make mortgages and business loans dearer, which cools spending in the same way a Fed rise would.
Officials signalled patience. Waller said rises need not come at back-to-back meetings. Jefferson said a decision may take more time.
The September rise needs time to work. It has only been six weeks.
against: Inflation is far from the goal. At 3.6% vs 2%, and the Fed itself calls progress insufficient.
Two officials dissented. Cook and Hammack voted to raise rates in October, showing strong appetite for tighter policy.
The economy looks strong. Q3 growth came in at 3.4%, meaning the economy can handle a higher rate.
choices.everyday: loan and savings rates stay roughly where they are for now. Markets now focus on December, where another rise remains a strong possibility.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 4.00%–4.25%
choices.meaning: the Fed presses the brake a little harder to show it is serious about bringing prices down.
for: Prices have been too high for over five years. Officials worry people will start to see high inflation as normal.
Energy is still expensive. Oil is near $103.37 a barrel and gasoline about $4.269 a gallon, so price pressure is still feeding through.
Dissenting votes. Two members wanted to raise in October, proving the committee is divided and eager to act.
Spending is strong. Shop sales jumped 0.8% in September, so demand is not fading on its own.
against: Hiring is weak. Two rises in a row while job growth is near zero could push companies to start cutting staff.
Officials said timing is flexible. They have openly said rises do not need to happen at every meeting.
choices.everyday: credit card and other variable loan rates would rise a little further. Savings accounts would pay a bit more.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate
choices.meaning: the Fed would switch from the brake to the gas, reversing its September decision.
for: Only in an emergency: for example a sudden market crash, a financial firm getting into serious trouble, or a sharp jump in layoffs.
against: The Fed just raised in September. Cutting now would confuse people and damage its credibility.
Inflation is moving the wrong way. Cutting would add fuel to rising prices.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but the surprise itself would likely signal that something had gone badly wrong in the economy.

change.lead: Our 75% / 23% / 2% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Some of it can move our view a lot. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro_title: Why upcoming reports matter for December
change.intro: The Fed just held in October. Now, every report released before the December meeting will shape whether the Fed decides to raise rates then. Here is what we are watching.

producer_price_index_ppi.why: Business costs today often become shop prices a few months later. It is an early warning.
producer_price_index_ppi.trigger: A big jump would add to the case for a December rise.

retail_sales.why: If spending stays strong, the economy can handle a higher rate, and demand keeps pushing prices up.
retail_sales.trigger: Another solid gain → leans toward a rise. A drop → leans toward hold.

weekly_jobless_claims.why: The fastest signal of layoffs. Right now it is very low (about 194,000).
weekly_jobless_claims.trigger: A steady climb toward 250,000 or more → hold firms up.

housing_starts.why: Housing reacts first to higher mortgage rates. A sharp fall would show the brake is already biting.
housing_starts.trigger: A big drop → leans toward hold.

durable_goods_orders.why: Shows whether businesses are still investing heavily.

gdp_q3_first_estimate_pce_pric.why: Key inputs for December to gauge summer growth and inflation.
gdp_q3_first_estimate_pce_pric.trigger: Stronger growth or hot PCE prices → raises chance of a December hike.

pce_prices_and_spending.why: The Fed's official inflation target is measured here.
pce_prices_and_spending.trigger: Core PCE staying around 3% or higher keeps pressure on the Fed.

employment_cost_index.why: Fast pay growth can keep service prices high.
employment_cost_index.trigger: Higher wage pressures support rate hikes.

job_openings_jolts.trigger: A sharp drop would signal labor cooling.

jobs_report.why: Will show whether September's weak hiring was a one-off or a trend.
jobs_report.trigger: Weak job gains again → hold; strong gains → raise.

consumer_price_index_cpi.why: Key early indicator of consumer price trends.
consumer_price_index_cpi.trigger: Hot CPI readings increase pressure for December.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Energy is the main driver of today's inflation. A new jump in oil would make a December rise more likely.
Bond market rates. If the 10-year yield falls back sharply, borrowing conditions loosen and a December hike becomes more likely.
Regional Fed bank presidents' speeches. Their comments will reveal how many officials share the view of the two dissenters.
A financial shock. A sudden market fall or trouble at a big financial firm would almost certainly push the Fed to hold.

report_card.one: Things cost 3.6% more than a year ago, far above the 2% goal.
report_card.look: The Fed's preferred price gauge (PCE, up 3.6%), the same gauge without food and energy (core PCE, up 3.1%), and consumer prices (CPI, up 3.7%).
report_card.why: The Fed's official measure (PCE) is well above the goal, both with and without energy, and prices have been above target for over five years. Energy is up 20.4% in a year. Business costs (PPI) are up 6.3%, which can reach shop shelves later.
report_card.change: Several months of core prices rising 0.2% a month or less, and energy prices falling back.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason the Fed raised rates in September and why two members dissented to raise in October.

report_card.one: Few people are losing jobs, but companies are hiring slowly.
report_card.look: New jobs each month, the unemployment rate, weekly claims for unemployment benefits, and job openings.
report_card.why: Good news: unemployment is low at 4.2%, and weekly layoff claims are very low (194,000). Bad news: only 29,000 jobs were added in September, and few workers are quitting to switch jobs, which shows low confidence.
report_card.change: Rising layoff claims or a jump in unemployment → red. Hiring picking back up above 100,000 a month → green.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason the Fed decided to wait in October. A weak job market makes another rate rise riskier.

report_card.one: The economy is growing at a solid pace, and people are still spending.
report_card.look: GDP (gross domestic product, the total value of everything the country produces), consumer spending and retail sales.
report_card.why: The economy grew at a 3.4% yearly pace in Q3, and an Atlanta Fed model estimates about 3.2% for the current quarter. Shop sales jumped 0.8% in September. Businesses are investing heavily, especially in artificial intelligence.
report_card.change: A sharp drop in spending or a weak official GDP number → yellow.
report_card.matters: A strong economy can handle higher rates, giving the Fed room to raise without causing a recession.

report_card.one: Borrowing costs jumped, but lenders are still lending calmly.
report_card.look: U.S. government bond rates (Treasury yields), the extra interest risky companies pay to borrow (credit spreads), and market expectations for inflation.
report_card.why: Worrying: the 10-year bond rate rose to 4.98%, making mortgages and loans more expensive. Reassuring: risky companies still borrow easily (spread of 3.14%), and investors still expect inflation of only about 2.35% a year over the long run.
report_card.change: Credit spreads widening sharply or stock markets falling hard → red. Bond rates settling down → green.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates are already slowing the economy, which is one reason the Fed paused in October.

consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.what: the government checks the prices of thousands of everyday things, like food, rent, gasoline, clothes, and doctor visits, and compares them with a year ago. A 3.7% rise means a $100 shopping basket now costs about $103.70.
consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.why: it is the most-watched price report in the country because it comes out first each month. It is 1.7 points above where the Fed wants prices to be.

core_cpi_without_food_and_energy.what: the same price check, but with food and energy removed. Those two jump up and down with weather, wars and harvests, so economists take them out to see the slower, steadier trend underneath.
core_cpi_without_food_and_energy.why: on a yearly basis this looks fairly calm at 2.6%, which shows the problem is mostly energy. But the monthly rise of 0.3% is a little fast.

cpi_energy.what: the price of gasoline, heating oil, electricity and natural gas for households.
cpi_energy.why: this is the main reason overall prices are high. A 20.4% jump in a year is very large. Energy also feeds into other prices.

cpi_shelter_housing_costs.what: the cost of rent, and an estimate of what homeowners would pay to rent their own home.
cpi_shelter_housing_costs.why: housing is the biggest single cost for most families, about a third of the CPI basket. A 3.2% rise is not alarming, but it is not low enough to help pull overall inflation down to 2%.

pce_prices_the_fed_s_official_target.what: the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, from the Commerce Department. Like CPI, it tracks prices, but it covers a wider range of spending.
pce_prices_the_fed_s_official_target.why: this is the number the Fed's 2% goal is actually based on. At 3.6%, it is 1.6 points above target.

core_pce_without_food_and_energy.what: the Fed's official price measure, with food and energy removed to show the underlying trend.
core_pce_without_food_and_energy.why: at 3.1%, it is still over a full percentage point above the goal, even after removing energy. That tells the Fed the problem is not only energy.

producer_price_index_ppi_final_demand.what: prices that businesses charge each other, for example what a factory charges a shop.
producer_price_index_ppi_final_demand.why: businesses usually pass higher costs on to customers, often a few months later. A 6.3% rise in business costs is an early warning.

10_year_inflation_expectation_from_bon.what: by comparing two kinds of government bonds (one protected against inflation and one not), we can work out how much inflation investors expect on average over the next 10 years.
10_year_inflation_expectation_from_bon.why: at 2.35%, investors still believe inflation will settle near 2–2.5% in the long run.

new_jobs_nonfarm_payrolls.what: the change in the number of people on company and government payrolls (farm jobs are counted separately).
new_jobs_nonfarm_payrolls.why: 29,000 is very low for an economy this size. It is the strongest reason the Fed paused in October.

unemployment_rate.what: the share of people who want a job, and are actively looking, but do not have one.
unemployment_rate.why: 4.2% is still low by historical standards, and Fed officials consider it close to maximum employment.

average_hourly_pay.what: the average hourly wage for workers.
average_hourly_pay.why: pay is rising about 3.0% while prices are rising faster, so many workers are slowly losing buying power.

labour_force_participation.what: the share of all adults who are either working or looking for work.
labour_force_participation.why: at 61.8%, it is steady, suggesting the low unemployment rate is genuine.

weekly_jobless_claims_new.what: how many people applied for unemployment benefits for the first time in a given week.
weekly_jobless_claims_new.why: at 194,000, this is very low. It shows companies are holding on to workers.

continuing_jobless_claims.what: the number of people still receiving unemployment benefits.
continuing_jobless_claims.why: at 1,701,000, if this keeps rising while new claims stay low, it means people who lose jobs are taking longer to find new ones.

job_openings_jolts.what: the number of jobs companies are trying to fill, from the JOLTS report.
job_openings_jolts.why: at 7.1 million, there are still open jobs, but the number is slowly falling.

quit_rate.what: the share of workers who quit their job in a month, usually to take a better one.
quit_rate.why: at 1.9%, workers are nervous about switching jobs.

real_gdp_growth_spring.what: GDP (gross domestic product) is the total value of everything the country produces, adjusted for inflation. 3.4% is the yearly pace in Q3.
real_gdp_growth_spring.why: well above the roughly 2% considered healthy and normal for the U.S.

gdpnow_model_estimate_summer.what: a computer model run by the Atlanta Fed that estimates GDP before the official number is released.
gdpnow_model_estimate_summer.why: 3.2% indicates strong current-quarter growth, supporting the view that the economy can handle higher rates.

retail_sales.what: total sales at shops, restaurants, petrol stations and online stores.
retail_sales.why: consumer spending is about two-thirds of the U.S. economy. A 0.8% monthly rise means demand is still robust.

real_consumer_spending.what: how much more people actually bought, after taking out the effect of higher prices.
real_consumer_spending.why: at +0.0% in the month, spending flattened out.

real_after_tax_income.what: the money people have left after taxes, adjusted for price rises.
real_after_tax_income.why: at −0.3% in the month, incomes dropped slightly after adjusting for inflation.

personal_saving_rate.what: the share of after-tax income that people save instead of spend.
personal_saving_rate.why: 3.8% is low, indicating families are stretching budgets due to high energy costs.

fed_s_target_range_federal_funds_rate.what: the interest rate banks charge each other for overnight loans. The Fed sets a range and keeps the actual rate inside it.
fed_s_target_range_federal_funds_rate.why: at 3.75%–4.00%, this is the main pedal the Fed controls.

effective_federal_funds_rate.what: the actual average rate banks paid each other for overnight loans, published by the New York Fed.
effective_federal_funds_rate.why: at 3.88%, it confirms the Fed's target range is working as intended.

3_month_treasury_bill.what: the interest rate the U.S. government pays to borrow for three months.
3_month_treasury_bill.why: at 4.18%, it remains above the Fed's target rate, reflecting expectations of further rate actions.

2_year_treasury_yield.what: the interest the government pays to borrow for two years.
2_year_treasury_yield.why: at 4.61%, this rate is driven by what investors think the Fed will do over the next two years.

10_year_treasury_yield.what: the interest the government pays to borrow for ten years.
10_year_treasury_yield.why: at 4.98%, mortgage rates and business loans follow this rate, making borrowing more expensive.

30_year_treasury_yield.what: the interest the government pays to borrow for thirty years.
30_year_treasury_yield.why: at 5.32%, it shows the long-term cost of government borrowing.

high_yield_credit_spread.what: the extra interest that riskier companies pay to borrow, on top of what the government pays.
high_yield_credit_spread.why: at 3.14%, it is low, meaning lenders are calm and businesses can still access credit.

fed_officials_end_2026_rate_forecast_d.what: four times a year, each of the 18 Fed officials writes down where they think the rate should be at the end of the year.
fed_officials_end_2026_rate_forecast_d.why: at 3.6%, it shows that officials expect further adjustments over time.

futures_market_odds_of_a_rise_by_decem.what: investors trade contracts that pay out based on future Fed rates. Governor Waller quoted futures traders seeing about an 85% chance of at least one rise by December.
futures_market_odds_of_a_rise_by_decem.why: markets strongly expect a rise by December.

now: Held in October, dissenters want rises
w: What it said: economic activity is expanding at a strong pace and inflation remains elevated, prompting the Committee to maintain the target range at 3-3/4 to 4 percent. Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack dissented, preferring a 1/4 point rise.
Why it matters: the Fed paused after its September hike, but two dissenting votes show that strong inflation is keeping pressure on officials to raise rates further.

said.pv: July: held, vote 9–3 (3 wanted a rise)
w: What it said: inflation remains elevated and the rise will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal.
Why it matters: the Fed moved from talking to acting. A unanimous vote showed broad agreement inside the Fed that prices were the priority.

said.v: Most expect another rise by year-end
w: What it is: a detailed summary of the discussion at the meeting, published three weeks later.
Why it matters: it shows most officials think another rise is likely this year, that many want insurance against stubborn inflation, and that each meeting is open.

said.v: further policy adjustments are likely to be needed
w: What he said: inflation risks have grown while job market risks have eased, so policy needs adjusting.
Why it matters: he expects more rises but did not say when. It supports the idea that the next move is up, not down.

said.v: Inflation too high for too long
w: What she said: she supported the September rise and wants to bring inflation down while keeping the job market strong.
Why it matters: her stance aligns with her subsequent October vote in favor of raising rates further.

said.v: A decision may take more time
w: What he said: bond rates have risen further since September, and the Fed will need to come to its own judgment.
Why it matters: this speech foreshadowed the Fed's decision to pause at the October meeting.

said.v: The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings
w: What he said: he expects more rises if the data come in as expected, but there is some flexibility about when those hikes will occur.
Why it matters: Waller clearly expected more rises while noting they do not have to happen at every consecutive meeting.

gaps: Market odds for December alone. We found no official source for exact December hike probabilities beyond general expectations. Why it matters: we cannot numerically compare our outlook with market pricing.
Chair Warsh's press conference transcript was not loaded, so we do not quote him directly. Why it matters: the Chair's tone is often the best single hint about future decisions.
Regional Fed bank presidents' speeches (other than Bowman, Waller, Jefferson, Cook, Barr) were not fully collected.
How we gathered data: every indicator value and date was read directly from the official sources linked in the facts section.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The Fed's goal is about 2% a year, measured by PCE. CPI is a similar measure that comes out earlier each month.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether people can find and keep work, the Fed's second job. A weak job market makes the Fed more careful about raising rates.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing and whether people are still spending. A strong economy can handle higher interest rates.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the Fed's own rate and the rates set by investors in financial markets. Market rates often move before the Fed does.
group_intros.said: Fed officials often hint at what they will do next. Reading their words carefully is one of the best ways to guess the next decision.
group_intros.global: The U.S. economy is affected by what happens elsewhere, especially energy prices and what other central banks do.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the Fed has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the Fed must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 13, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.

summary.headline: PCE inflation rose to 3.6% in September, and Q3 economic growth came in at a strong 3.4% annual pace.
items: PCE prices (the Fed's official target) increased from +3.4% to +3.6% in the year to September.
Core PCE (without food and energy) edged up from +3.0% to +3.1% in the year to September.
Real GDP growth for Q3 2026 was reported at 3.4% (yearly pace) on Oct 29, 2026.
Real consumer spending flattened to +0.0% in September, while real after-tax income dipped −0.3%.
